question: Can RL policy networks be trained to form automatically detectable, functionally specialized modules that are understandable and causally testable at a higher level than individual neurons?

key_findings.claim: Distance-weighted connection-cost regularization plus neuron relocation induces sparse, spatially localized policy modules.
key_findings.evidence: The method embeds MLP neurons in 2D, penalizes log-scaled weight magnitude by connection distance, periodically swaps high-degree neurons to lower cost, and prunes/fine-tunes after 80% of training. Ablations attribute isolation to regularization, distance weighting and relocation in different proportions.

key_findings.claim: The extended Louvain procedure aligns weight communities with activation-correlation communities substantially better than standard Louvain on the studied MLPs.
key_findings.evidence: Its internal and fine-tuned variants address input fan-out and layer fragmentation. Across three MiniGrid tasks and ten seeds, fine-tuned variants reach isolation around 0.94-0.95 and ARI up to roughly 0.83 at strong regularization, whereas weight-only Louvain has lower ARI.

anchors.section: Sections 3.4-3.5, functional alignment and extended Louvain

key_findings.claim: Module interventions provide causal evidence for axis-specific navigation functions.
key_findings.evidence: Negative saturation or sign negation of selected communities sharply redistributes action frequencies along the corresponding x, y or z direction and reduces return; the appendix reports full action and outcome statistics for 3D-DO and Go-to-Key policies.

key_findings.claim: The method exposes a Pong shortcut but remains a small-network demonstration with a performance-interpretability tradeoff.
key_findings.evidence: A 37-parameter policy can score 21 in the symbolic Pong setup, yet it relies on the opponent position; retraining without that feature restores robustness. Stronger regularization eventually collapses sparsity and return, and the training modifications add 17% runtime.

method.core_idea: Build interpretability into an RL policy by encouraging local sparse connectivity, detecting structural communities and validating their function through activation alignment and interventions.
method.mechanism: Train PPO MLPs with a distance-weighted logarithmic connection penalty and periodic neuron swaps, prune and fine-tune, partition the resulting graph with an internal/fine-tuned Louvain variant, compare partitions with correlation-based ARI, then ablate or negate modules.
assumptions: Useful policy computation decomposes into sparse modules that can tolerate an architectural penalty.
Euclidean neuron placement and connection length are meaningful training biases.
Activation correlation is an adequate proxy for functional modularity.
Module interventions are sufficiently localized to support functional attribution.

techniques.role: Permutes units so important paths become spatially cheap.
Detects depth-spanning communities in directed layerwise MLP graphs.
Compares structural partitions with functional activation partitions.
Tests behavioral specialization through causal parameter changes.

evaluations.setting: Dynamic Obstacles, 3D Dynamic Obstacles and Go-to-Key MiniGrid PPO policies over ten seeds.
evaluations.metric: Return, sparsity, module isolation and adjusted Rand index.
evaluations.result: Localized modules consistently correspond to navigation axes; stronger regularization improves isolation/alignment until return deteriorates.
evaluations.baseline: Vanilla PPO, standard Louvain, correlation Louvain, and ablations without distance weighting or relocation.

evaluations.setting: Targeted module interventions in selected MiniGrid policies.
evaluations.metric: Action frequency, failure/success outcome and episode return.
evaluations.result: Interventions selectively suppress or dominate the action axis attributed to each community and reduce return.
evaluations.baseline: The unmodified network; only a small number of representative policies receive detailed interventions.

evaluations.setting: Symbolic-observation Pong with a deterministic follow-ball opponent.
evaluations.metric: Game score, remaining parameter count and robustness after removing opponent position.
evaluations.result: Perfect score is retained with 37 parameters in one regime; module inspection confirms a brittle opponent-position shortcut and retraining removes it.
evaluations.baseline: Unregularized 435-parameter policy and prior SCoBot diagnosis of the same shortcut.

limitations: Evidence centers on two-layer MLPs and small symbolic MiniGrid/Pong tasks, not modern deep RL policies.
Regularization can reduce return and eventually produces structural collapse.
Activation collection uses 10,000 episodes and may become costly at scale.
ARI between two heuristic partitions is not direct proof of semantic modularity.
Neuron permutation, pruning thresholds, placement scale and regularization schedule add several choices.
Human interpretation is still required to name module functions after discovery.
Pong uses a custom symbolic environment and deterministic opponent, limiting external validity.
failure_modes: A task needs distributed shared features, so forcing locality destroys performance or creates misleading modules.
Louvain divides a true computation across layers or merges modules through high-fan-out inputs.
Correlated activations arise from shared observations rather than shared function.
An intervention changes downstream scale broadly, producing apparent specialization without a clean causal mechanism.
A high-performing policy exploits environment shortcuts that are invisible under the training distribution.
reusable_insights: Evaluate inherent interpretability jointly with return; a clean graph is not useful if task competence collapses.
Structural modules should be checked against functional activity and targeted interventions.
Environment perturbations are essential for distinguishing genuine strategy from shortcut dependence.
Module stability across seeds is a key prerequisite for scalable human interpretation.
open_questions: Does the method scale to convolutional, recurrent or transformer policies with shared representations?
Can module functions be labeled automatically without treating correlation as ground truth?
How stable are partitions under seeds, environment shifts and community-detection hyperparameters?
Can modularity be induced without a return penalty or expensive activation collection?

competitive_landscape.title: Seeing is Believing: Brain-Inspired Modular Training for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: BIMT introduces connection-cost regularization and neuron relocation for visually modular supervised networks; the reviewed paper extends these ideas to RL, automated community detection and causal module characterization.

competitive_landscape.title: Evaluating Brain-Inspired Modular Training in Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: This audit asks whether BIMT actually assists automated circuit discovery, while the reviewed work proposes a specialized graph-partition pipeline and evaluates functional alignment in RL policies.

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretable Concept Bottlenecks to Align Reinforcement Learning Agents
competitive_landscape.difference: SCoBots impose human-named object and relational concepts and already diagnose the Pong shortcut; neural modules require fewer predefined concepts but yield less immediately legible semantics.

competitive_landscape.title: Interpretable and Editable Programmatic Tree Policies for Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: INTERPRETER distills black-box policies into compact editable programs; the reviewed approach preserves a neural policy while inducing and intervening on internal modules.

novelty_assessment: The integration of modular training, neural-network-aware Louvain detection, correlation alignment and intervention is a meaningful RL interpretability pipeline. The evidence is promising but preliminary: the networks are tiny, the semantic labeling remains human-driven, and direct predecessors already supply both the training bias and the highlighted Pong failure case.
